conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Thank you for making time to talk with me today. I know how full-on new-mother life can feel, so I really appreciate you being here.

I’d like to check in with you using a short questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a simple, 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past week. It’s not a test of your parenting or of you as a person; it’s just a way for us to see how best to support you right now.

Everything you share is confidential within our clinical team, and there are no right or wrong answers. We’ll go through each question one at a time, and you can answer in your own words. If anything feels uncomfortable, we can pause or skip it—this is your space, and I want it to feel as safe and supportive as possible.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Honestly, it’s kind of…dulled. I still get little sparks—like when the baby grips my finger or when my toddler brings me a picture he colored—but they fade fast. It’s like I can recognize “oh, this should feel really nice,” yet the warm bit doesn’t last. Most of the day I’m just going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Um… maybe every couple of days something will make me crack a smile, but it’s pretty half-hearted. My partner tried to joke with me yesterday and I sort of forced a laugh, then felt guilty because it wasn’t real. So, no, I’m not really laughing the way I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to—like, I’ll tell myself, “Tomorrow I’ll enjoy that walk,” or “I’m looking forward to coffee with my friend”—but when the moment comes, it just feels… flat. Most mornings I wake up already tired and a little tense, so the looking-forward part doesn’t really happen. I still plan things, but the excitement isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking, “I must be missing some cue,” or “If I were better at this, he’d sleep.” It’s not constant, but little stuff like that pops into my head a few times a week, even when I know it’s not really my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly it circles around the baby—like I’ll lie down and suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds normal, or I’ll replay whether I buckled the car seat tight enough. There’s no real reason, but the worry still shows up and my heart races for a bit until I distract myself. It’s not all day, but it hits several times a week.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s not every day, but a couple of times this week I’ll be feeding the baby in the rocker and suddenly feel this rush—like my chest tightens and I think, “What if I can’t handle this?” It passes after a minute or two, but in the moment it feels like I need to bolt somewhere, even though there’s nothing to run from.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… especially in the evenings when both kids are fussy and the house is a mess. I’ll look around and feel like I’m drowning in small chores. Most nights I still get everything done, but it’s with this heavy, “I can’t keep up” feeling. I manage, but I’m running on empty by the time I finally sit down.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not every night, but probably three or four times this week I’ve laid down feeling wired and teary. My mind just keeps looping—mostly about whether I’m doing enough for the kids, or I’ll fixate on the baby’s breathing monitor. I’ll finally drift off around two or three, then wake up at five when my toddler calls out. So I’m not sleeping great, but it’s not every single night.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… it kind of comes in waves. I’ll be fine for a while, then out of nowhere I’ll feel this heavy sadness settle in—like yesterday, just folding laundry, and I had to stop because I suddenly wanted to cry. It’s not every moment, but it’s been happening most days this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not full-on crying—more like my eyes sting and I have to blink hard to stop tears. It happened twice this week: once when the baby wouldn’t latch and once when I spilled pumped milk. I didn’t actually sob, but I felt that lump in my throat and had to sit down so I didn’t leak tears in front of my toddler.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

It sounds like the last couple of weeks have felt heavy and colourless. You're working so hard to stay on top of feedings, naps, housework and your toddler's needs, yet the spark of joy that used to come easily now slips away quickly. You described waves of sadness catching you off-guard, worries about the baby racing through your mind at night, and moments when your chest tightens with panic even though nothing dangerous is happening. At the same time you're aware that these feelings aren't your usual self, and you're doing your best to push through for your children.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes almost no genuine laughter, forced smiles, and loss of previous ability to find things funny, aligning with 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient actively tries to anticipate enjoyment but consistently feels "flat" and lacks excitement, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms self-blame "some of the time" with clear examples of unwarranted guilt about baby's sleep, occurring a few times weekly.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, intrusive worries about the baby several times a week without real cause, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of sudden fear/panic multiple times this week without clear trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports consistent struggle ('drowning,' 'can't keep up') but still managing tasks, aligning with 'sometimes not coping as well as usual.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple nights (3-4) of significant sleep disruption directly linked to emotional distress, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, recurrent waves of sadness affecting daily activities most days, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 19 on the EPDS places you well above the 14-point cut-off that signals probable major depression in the postpartum period. You endorsed core symptoms meeting DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset: depressed mood most days (<quote>heavy sadness</quote>), loss of interest or pleasure (<quote>flat</quote>, <quote>excitement isn't there</quote>), significant self-reproach, sleep disruption linked to mood, and observable tearfulness. Several of these symptoms occur within the required 2-week window and cause clear functional difficulty. In addition you describe recurrent, unprovoked panic sensations (<sym>chest tightens</sym>, urge to flee) and multiple weekly episodes of excessive worry about infant safety, consistent with comorbid postpartum anxiety. Item 10 was scored 0, so acute self-harm risk is not indicated at present, but the overall burden of depressive and anxious symptoms warrants prompt clinical assessment and treatment planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med> or local <med>perinatal mental-health clinic</med> to review results and discuss treatment options
2. Request a full evaluation for <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> and possible <med>anxiety disorders</med>; bring a copy of your EPDS responses
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and, if needed, antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding
4. Involve a trusted adult who can help with overnight infant care so you can obtain 4-5 hour stretches of sleep; improved sleep often lessens mood and panic symptoms
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress once treatment begins
6. Keep the 24-hr <med>Postpartum Support International</med> warm-line number handy: 1-800-944-4773 (text 800-944-4773 English or 971-203-7773 Spanish) for peer support and local-resource referrals
7. Continue monitoring: if thoughts of self-harm or harm to baby ever arise, seek emergency care immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, interviewed 12 days after delivery, 2nd child  

Presenting symptoms endorsed:  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness most days, joylessness (“flat,” “heavy”)  
- Marked anhedonia: no genuine laughter, anticipatory pleasure absent  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re parenting competence, several ×/week  
- Recurrent, intrusive anxious worries about infant safety; associated panic-like surges 2–3 ×/week (chest tightness, urge to flee)  
- Evening “drowning” feeling; difficulty coping with routine demands  
- Initial insomnia 3–4 nights/week driven by rumination and vigilance  
- No self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)  

Pattern: Symptoms present > half the days in past week, interfere with functioning, worse in evenings; no psychotic features or suicidal thoughts.  

Screening significance:  
High endorsement for core depressive items (mood, anhedonia, tearfulness, guilt) plus prominent anxiety/panic symptoms; meets threshold for probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety, moderate severity.  

Risk factors:  
- Sleep deprivation linked to mood  
- High self-criticism / perfectionism  
- Absence of self-harm intent (protective)  

Plan:  
Recommend formal clinical assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and prompt referral to perinatal mental health specialty for evaluation and possible evidence-based intervention (CBT or medication discussion). Continue monitoring safety at every contact.
